claim: Autotransporters are a superfamily of bacterial virulence factors consisting of an N-terminal extracellular ('passenger') domain and a C-terminal β barrel ('β') domain that resides in the outer membrane (OM).
source: Autotransporters are a superfamily of bacterial virulence factors consisting of an N-terminal extracellular ('passenger') domain and a C-terminal β barrel ('β') domain that resides in the outer membrane (OM).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about autotransporters that represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: A conserved OM protein insertase (the Bam complex) and a molecular chaperone (SurA) are both necessary and sufficient to promote the complete assembly of the Escherichia coli O157:H7 autotransporter EspP in vitro.
source: Here we show that a conserved OM protein insertase (the Bam complex) and a molecular chaperone (SurA) are both necessary and sufficient to promote the complete assembly of the Escherichia coli O157:H7 autotransporter EspP in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The membrane integration of the β domain is the rate-limiting step in autotransporter assembly.
source: Our results indicate that the membrane integration of the β domain is the rate-limiting step in autotransporter assembly and that passenger domain translocation does not require the input of external energy.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by kinetic analysis data presented in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Passenger domain translocation does not require the input of external energy.
source: Our results indicate that the membrane integration of the β domain is the rate-limiting step in autotransporter assembly and that passenger domain translocation does not require the input of external energy.
evidence: This is supported by the successful reconstitution of autotransporter assembly in vitro without ATP or membrane potential.

claim: Autotransporter assembly is catalyzed by a single copy of the Bam complex.
source: Furthermore, experiments using nanodiscs strongly suggest that autotransporter assembly is catalyzed by a single copy of the Bam complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from nanodisc reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The autotransporter (type Va) pathway is the most widespread virulence factor secretion pathway in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: The autotransporter (type Va) pathway is the most widespread virulence factor secretion pathway in Gram-negative bacteria (Leyton et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Leyton et al., 2012.

claim: Passenger domains vary widely in sequence and size (∼20–400 kD), but almost always form an unusual repetitive structure known as a β helix.
source: Passenger domains vary widely in sequence and size (∼20–400 kD), but almost always form an unusual repetitive structure known as a β helix (Junker et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Junker et al., 2006.

claim: β domains are typically ∼30 kD in size and fold into a β barrel structure.
source: β domains are typically ∼30 kD in size and, like the vast majority of bacterial integral OM proteins, fold into a β barrel structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β domain structure.

claim: The structures of all of the β domains that have been solved to date are nearly superimposable.
source: While the sequences of β domains are also very heterogeneous, the structures of all of the β domains that have been solved to date are nearly superimposable (Oomen et al., 2004; Barnard et al., 2007; van den Berg, 2010; Zhai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural studies.

claim: After autotransporters are translocated across the inner membrane (IM) through the Sec complex they interact with molecular chaperones that presumably maintain them in an assembly-competent state.
source: After autotransporters are translocated across the inner membrane (IM) through the Sec complex they interact with molecular chaperones that presumably maintain them in an assembly-competent state (Ieva and Bernstein, 2009; Ruiz-Perez et al., 2009; Ieva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The β domain is targeted to the Bam complex, an essential heterooligomer consisting of an integral OM protein (BamA) and four lipoproteins (BamBCDE) that catalyzes the membrane insertion of β barrel proteins.
source: Subsequently the β domain is targeted to the Bam complex, an essential heterooligomer consisting of an integral OM protein (BamA) and four lipoproteins (BamBCDE) that catalyzes the membrane insertion of β barrel proteins (Voulhoux et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2005; Sauri et al., 2009; Hagan et al., 2010; Ieva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: X-ray crystallographic analysis suggests that the BamA β barrel domain is unstable and may open laterally to allow the escape of client proteins into the lipid bilayer.
source: X-ray crystallographic analysis suggests that the BamA β barrel domain is unstable and may open laterally to allow the escape of client proteins into the lipid bilayer (Noinaj et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystallographic studies.

claim: The passenger domain is translocated across the OM in a C-to-N-terminal fashion.
source: Although it has been shown that the passenger domain is translocated across the OM in a C-to-N-terminal fashion (Ieva and Bernstein, 2009; Junker et al., 2009), the mechanism of translocation is poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of the β domain abolishes passenger domain translocation.
source: Based on the observation that deletion of the β domain abolishes passenger domain translocation, it was originally proposed that the β domain serves as the transport channel for the passenger domain (whence the name 'autotransporter') (Pohlner et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pohlner et al., 1987.

claim: Upon completion of translocation the two domains are connected by an α-helical linker that is embedded inside the β domain pore.
source: At first glance, this hypothesis seems to be supported by crystallographic studies showing that upon completion of translocation the two domains are connected by an α-helical linker that is embedded inside the β domain pore (Oomen et al., 2004; Barnard et al., 2007; van den Berg, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystallographic studies.

claim: The β domain pore is only ∼10 Å in diameter.
source: The same studies, however, revealed that the β domain pore is only ∼10 Å in diameter.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic data from cited studies.

claim: The polypeptide that resides inside the β domain forms an α helix prior to the completion of translocation.
source: On the contrary, available evidence indicates that the polypeptide that resides inside the β domain forms an α helix prior to the completion of translocation (Ieva et al., 2008; Peterson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Small folded polypeptides have been shown to be secreted efficiently by the autotransporter pathway.
source: Furthermore, small folded polypeptides have been shown to be secreted efficiently by the autotransporter pathway and a subset of naturally occurring passenger domains undergo disulfide bonding in the periplasm (Skillman et al., 2005; Jong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A subset of naturally occurring passenger domains undergo disulfide bonding in the periplasm.
source: Furthermore, small folded polypeptides have been shown to be secreted efficiently by the autotransporter pathway and a subset of naturally occurring passenger domains undergo disulfide bonding in the periplasm (Skillman et al., 2005; Jong et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BamA has been shown to interact with the passenger domain during the translocation reaction.
source: Finally, BamA has been shown to interact with the passenger domain during the translocation reaction (Ieva and Bernstein, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The β domain does appear to play a role in translocation.
source: While the β domain does appear to play a role in translocation (Saurí et al., 2011; Pavlova et al., 2013), these and other results strongly suggest that autotransporter assembly is more complex than originally envisioned.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The periplasm is devoid of ATP and there is no membrane potential across the bacterial OM.
source: Although most protein translocation reactions require external energy in the form of ATP or a membrane potential, the periplasm is devoid of ATP and there is no membrane potential across the bacterial OM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell structure.

claim: The sequential folding of segments of the β helix in the extracellular space drives translocation and prevents retrograde movement into the periplasm.
source: To explain the energetics of secretion, it has been proposed that the sequential folding of segments of the β helix in the extracellular space drives translocation and prevents retrograde movement into the periplasm (Klauser et al., 1992; Junker et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous studies cited.

claim: Mutations that impair the folding of C-terminal segments of two different passenger domains significantly reduce the efficiency of secretion.
source: Consistent with this vectorial folding model, mutations that impair the folding of C-terminal segments of two different passenger domains significantly reduce the efficiency of secretion (Peterson et al., 2010; Renn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations that perturb the folding of medial and N-terminal segments of the passenger domain produce only a modest translocation defect.
source: Mutations that perturb the folding of medial and N-terminal segments of the passenger domain, however, produce only a modest translocation defect (Kang'ethe and Bernstein, 2013b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The intrinsically disordered receptor domain (RD) of the Bordetella pertussis RTX toxin has been shown to be secreted efficiently by the autotransporter pathway.
source: Furthermore, the intrinsically disordered receptor domain (RD) of the Bordetella pertussis RTX toxin has been shown to be secreted efficiently by the autotransporter pathway (Kang'ethe and Bernstein, 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The presence of a large number of acidic residues is critical for the secretion of the RD.
source: Interestingly, the presence of a large number of acidic residues is critical for the secretion of the RD.
evidence: This is based on previous findings about the RD domain.

claim: Naturally occurring passenger domains are predominantly acidic.
source: This observation, together with the finding that naturally occurring passenger domains are predominantly acidic, suggests that charge interactions may play a significant role in driving the translocation reaction.
evidence: This is an observation about passenger domain composition.

claim: Following the completion of translocation, the passenger domain of EspP and other members of the SPATE family is released in an unusual intrabarrel cleavage reaction that requires accurate folding of the β domain and precise positioning of the passenger domain-β domain junction.
source: Following the completion of translocation, the passenger domain of EspP and other members of the SPATE (serine protease autotransporters of Enterobacteriaceae) family is released in an unusual intrabarrel cleavage reaction that requires accurate folding of the β domain and precise positioning of the passenger domain-β domain junction (Dautin et al., 2007; Barnard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The insertion of small E. coli β barrel proteins such as OmpT and OmpA into proteoliposomes can be catalyzed by the purified Bam complex and the periplasmic chaperone SurA.
source: Although it was previously shown that the insertion of small E. coli β barrel proteins such as OmpT and OmpA into proteoliposomes can be catalyzed by the purified Bam complex and the periplasmic chaperone SurA (Hagan et al., 2010; Hagan and Kahne, 2011; Hagan et al., 2013), we did not observe assembly of EspP using the same methodology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Large N-terminal segments of autotransporter passenger domains can be deleted without affecting the integration of the β domain into the OM or the secretion of the remaining passenger domain fragment.
source: It has long been known that large N-terminal segments of autotransporter passenger domains can be deleted without affecting the integration of the β domain into the OM or the secretion of the remaining passenger domain fragment (Dautin and Bernstein, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The native EspP passenger domain is 968 residues in length.
source: The native EspP passenger domain is 968 residues in length (Figure 1A), but a derivative that contains only 26 residues of the ∼28 residue C-terminal segment that reside inside the β domain in an α-helical conformation (EspPΔ5) is assembled as efficiently as the wild-type protein in vivo (Pavlova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: EspPΔ5 is assembled as efficiently as the wild-type protein in vivo.
source: The native EspP passenger domain is 968 residues in length (Figure 1A), but a derivative that contains only 26 residues of the ∼28 residue C-terminal segment that reside inside the β domain in an α-helical conformation (EspPΔ5) is assembled as efficiently as the wild-type protein in vivo (Pavlova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pavlova et al., 2013.

claim: The modification or deletion of residues in the α-helical segment can profoundly perturb the folding and integration of the β domain into the OM and/or the proteolytic release of the passenger domain.
source: The modification or deletion of residues in the α-helical segment, however, can profoundly perturb the folding and integration of the β domain into the OM and/or the proteolytic release of the passenger domain, which requires precise alignment of the cleavage junction with key catalytic residues (Dautin et al., 2007; Ieva et al., 2008; Barnard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The accurate assembly of EspP(46+β) results in the proteolytic release of the 46 residue passenger domain and the accumulation of a folded ∼30 kD β domain that is resistant to SDS denaturation unless heated.
source: We expected that the accurate assembly of EspP(46+β) would result in the proteolytic release of the 46 residue passenger domain and the accumulation of a folded ∼30 kD β domain that, as previously shown, is resistant to SDS denaturation unless heated (Skillman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an expectation based on previous findings cited.

claim: OmpT folds into a stable structure that is enzymatically active and resistant to SDS denaturation in the presence of proteoliposomes and a molar excess of SurA.
source: In the presence of the proteoliposomes and a molar excess of SurA, denatured OmpT folds into a stable structure that is enzymatically active and resistant to SDS denaturation.
evidence: This describes the expected outcome of the OmpT folding assay.

claim: BamABCDE stimulated the assembly of EspP(46+β).
source: Interestingly, we found that BamABCDE also stimulated the assembly of EspP(46+β).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: A rapidly migrating (∼27 kD) band that corresponds to the folded form of the free EspP β domain appeared within 5 min.
source: A rapidly migrating (∼27 kD) band that corresponds to the folded form of the free EspP β domain appeared within 5 min and was more prominent at later time points when the samples were not heated (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No proteolytic processing was observed if either SurA or BamABCDE was omitted from the reaction.
source: No proteolytic processing was observed if either SurA or BamABCDE was omitted from the reaction or if BamAB or BamCDE subomplexes were used in place of the holocomplex (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: BamABDE and BamACDE both promoted the assembly EspP(46+β), but less effectively than BamABCDE.
source: BamABDE and BamACDE both promoted the assembly EspP(46+β), but less effectively than BamABCDE (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The addition of purified Skp to reactions containing BamABCDE and SurA inhibited EspP(46+β) assembly.
source: Finally, the addition of purified Skp to reactions containing BamABCDE and SurA inhibited EspP(46+β) assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and ATP (0.1 mM) blocked assembly altogether (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: ATP (0.1 mM) blocked assembly altogether.
source: Finally, the addition of purified Skp to reactions containing BamABCDE and SurA inhibited EspP(46+β) assembly (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and ATP (0.1 mM) blocked assembly altogether (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments.

claim: EspP derivatives that have passenger domains ranging in size from 72–734 residues were all processed with approximately the same efficiency as EspP(46+β).
source: As Western blot analysis using the anti-EspP C-terminal antiserum indicated, EspP derivatives that have passenger domains ranging in size from 72–734 residues were all processed with approximately the same efficiency as EspP(46+β) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: After incubating EspP(96+β) with proteoliposomes containing BamABCDE and SurA for 30 min, the cleaved β domain was both subject to heat denaturation in SDS and resistant to proteinase K (PK) digestion.
source: Initially we found that after incubating EspP(96+β) with proteoliposomes containing BamABCDE and SurA for 30 min, the cleaved β domain was both subject to heat denaturation in SDS and resistant to proteinase K (PK) digestion (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The β domain was not only properly folded, but also inserted into the proteoliposomes.
source: This result provided direct evidence that the β domain was not only properly folded, but also inserted into the proteoliposomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PK resistance data.

claim: The passenger domain was translocated into the lumen of the proteoliposomes.
source: The finding that the ∼35 kDa polypeptide was resistant to PK digestion unless detergent was added showed that the passenger domain was translocated into the lumen of the proteoliposomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PK resistance data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The epitope tag is the last segment of the protein that traverses the membrane.
source: Because the epitope tag is the last segment of the protein that traverses the membrane, these results confirm that the translocation reaction went to completion.
evidence: This is based on the known directionality of translocation and the position of the HA tag.

claim: EspP(HA-251+β) was processed at a very similar rate to EspP(46+β).
source: Interestingly, EspP(HA-251+β) was processed at a very similar rate (Figure 6C, top and Figure 6D, blue curve).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The rate constants obtained by fitting the assembly data for the two EspP derivatives to either a single exponential or two-step model were nearly identical.
source: Indeed the rate constants obtained by fitting the assembly data for the two EspP derivatives to either a single exponential or two-step model were nearly identical (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on kinetic analysis of the data.

claim: A PK-resistant ∼30 kD polypeptide that corresponds to the cleaved passenger domain accumulated in parallel with the cleaved β domain.
source: In the case of the EspP(HA-251+β) derivative, a PK-resistant ∼30 kD polypeptide that corresponds to the cleaved passenger domain accumulated in parallel with the cleaved β domain (Figure 6E, top).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The G1066A mutation caused a similar delay in the assembly of both EspP derivatives in vitro.
source: The mutation caused a similar delay in the assembly of both EspP derivatives in vitro (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Defects in the folding of the β domain affect the ability of the Bam complex to catalyze subsequent steps in EspP assembly.
source: This observation corroborates the conclusion that defects in the folding of the β domain affect the ability of the Bam complex to catalyze subsequent steps in EspP assembly.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the G1066A mutation data.

claim: EspP(HA-714+β) was processed only slightly more slowly than EspP(46+β).
source: Despite the presence of a much larger passenger domain, EspP(HA-714+β) was processed only slightly more slowly than EspP(46+β) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the kinetic data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Passenger domain translocation is relatively fast, and the assembly of the β domain is the rate-limiting step in autotransporter biogenesis.
source: Taken together, the results indicate that passenger domain translocation is relatively fast, and that the assembly of the β domain is the rate-limiting step in autotransporter biogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kinetic data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The introduction of a short linker into EspP(HA-714+β) that impairs passenger domain folding and stalls translocation in vivo only modestly affected assembly in vitro.
source: Curiously, the introduction of a short linker into EspP(HA-714+β) that impairs passenger domain folding and stalls translocation in vivo (Ieva and Bernstein, 2009) only modestly affected assembly in vitro (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of an exogenous energy source translocation is not driven exclusively by protein folding.
source: This observation, along with the finding that an EspP chimera containing a >200 residue intrinsically disordered passenger domain segment that is secreted efficiently in vivo could also assemble in the in vitro assay (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), suggests that in the absence of an exogenous energy source translocation is not driven exclusively by protein folding.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data on folding-deficient and disordered passenger domains.

claim: Both EspP(46+β) and EspP(HA-251+β) were assembled into nanodiscs about as efficiently as they were assembled into proteoliposomes.
source: Western blot analysis using the anti-EspP C-terminal antiserum revealed that both EspP(46+β) and EspP(HA-251+β) were assembled into nanodiscs about as efficiently as they were assembled into proteoliposomes (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The curvature of the proteoliposome membrane is not itself required for the assembly process.
source: These results not only provide evidence that a Bam complex monomer is sufficient to catalyze autotransporter assembly, but also show that the curvature of the proteoliposome membrane is not itself required for the assembly process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the successful assembly in nanodiscs.

claim: Passenger domain secretion does not require either an input of exogenous energy or the presence of IM proteins that transduce energy from the cytoplasm or the membrane potential.
source: Our work demonstrates that passenger domain secretion does not require either an input of exogenous energy or the presence of IM proteins that transduce energy from the cytoplasm or the membrane potential.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful reconstitution with only purified components.

claim: ATP hydrolysis is required to drive protein translocation through the Sec complex in an analogous reconstituted assay system.
source: The results are surprising because ATP hydrolysis is required to drive protein translocation through the Sec complex in an analogous reconstituted assay system (Brundage et al., 1990) and because other types of protein translocation reactions appear to require a significant energy expenditure (Alder and Theg, 2003; Shi and Theg, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The folding of the passenger domain in the extracellular space has been shown to play a role in driving translocation in vivo.
source: In the autotransporter pathway, the folding of the passenger domain in the extracellular space has been shown to play a role in driving translocation in vivo, and folding may also promote translocation in the in vitro assay.
evidence: This is based on previous findings about the role of folding.

claim: Electrostatic or other types of interactions between passenger domains and the Bam complex or membrane lipids may facilitate translocation.
source: As previously suggested (Kang'ethe and Bernstein, 2013a), electrostatic or other types of interactions between passenger domains and the Bam complex or membrane lipids may facilitate translocation.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on previous work.

claim: The Bam complex might guide passenger domains along a low-energy pathway.
source: Like the FimD protein that secretes type I pilus subunits, the Bam complex might also guide passenger domains along a low-energy pathway (Geibel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion based on analogy to FimD.

claim: The Bam complex might catalyze at least the initial stages of translocation and the assembly of the β domain in a concerted fashion.
source: Alternatively, the Bam complex might catalyze at least the initial stages of translocation and the assembly of the β domain in a concerted fashion.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism.

claim: Stalled translocation reactions can be restarted in vivo.
source: While the coupling of translocation to β domain assembly might also explain the assembly of a folding-deficient mutant such as EspP(HA-714+β)586TEV in vitro, the observation that stalled translocation reactions can be restarted in vivo (Ieva and Bernstein, 2009; JHP and HDB, unpublished results) strongly suggests that energy can be harnessed after the insertion of the β domain is largely complete.
evidence: This is based on a citation and unpublished results.

claim: Pulse-chase labeling and photocrosslinking experiments have previously provided evidence that β domain assembly is slower than passenger domain translocation in vivo.
source: Pulse-chase labeling and photocrosslinking experiments have previously provided evidence that β domain assembly is slower than passenger domain translocation in vivo (Ieva et al., 2011), but the interpretation of these experiments is complicated by the fact that the synthesis of the 1300 residue EspP protein is itself rather slow (∼45 s).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Long passenger domain segments fold slowly and consequently resist aggregation, at least in vitro.
source: This observation corroborates the conclusion that even long passenger domain segments fold slowly and consequently resist aggregation, at least in vitro (Junker et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: The β domain clearly interacts with Skp in vivo.
source: Furthermore, given that the β domain clearly interacts with Skp in vivo (Ieva et al., 2011; Pavlova et al., 2013), it is striking that the presence of the chaperone inhibited assembly in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: BamABCDE was more active than Bam(AB)(CDE).
source: It is striking that, at least in our hands, BamABCDE was more active than Bam(AB)(CDE).
evidence: This is an observation from the OmpT folding assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The structure of the Bam complex assembled in vivo differs from that of the Bam complex reconstructed from BamAB and BamCDE subcomplexes in vitro.
source: While this disparity may simply be due to technical issues, our results also raise the possibility that the structure of the Bam complex assembled in vivo differs from that of the Bam complex reconstructed from BamAB and BamCDE subcomplexes in vitro.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the activity difference.

claim: The Bam complex remains intact in vivo and does not undergo a dynamic cycle in which BamAB and BamCDE subcomplexes rapidly dissociate and reassociate.
source: In this regard it should be noted that in preliminary experiments we obtained evidence that the Bam complex remains intact in vivo and does not undergo a dynamic cycle in which BamAB and BamCDE subcomplexes rapidly dissocate and reassociate (JHP and HDB, unpublished results).
evidence: This is based on unpublished preliminary data.

claim: EspP consists of a signal peptide (SP; residues 1–55), an extracellular ('passenger') domain (residues 56–1023) and a β barrel ('β') domain (residues 1024–1300).
source: (A) EspP consists of a signal peptide (SP; residues 1–55), an extracellular ('passenger') domain (residues 56–1023) and a β barrel ('β') domain (residues 1024–1300) (Brunder et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, with a citation.

claim: Most of the passenger domain forms a long β helix, while the N-terminus (residues 56–313) forms a discrete globular domain.
source: While most of the passenger domain forms a long β helix, the N-terminus (residues 56–313) forms a discrete globular domain (Khan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A, with a citation.

claim: Prior to the release of the passenger domain in an intrabarrel cleavage reaction, ∼28 residues of the 46 residue passenger domain are embedded inside the β domain pore.
source: (B) Illustration of EspP(46+β). Prior to the release of the passenger domain in an intrabarrel cleavage reaction, ∼28 residues of the 46 residue passenger domain are embedded inside the β domain pore.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The EspP passenger domain is secreted in a hairpin conformation while distinct regions of the β domain interact with BamA, BamB and BamD.
source: (C) Available evidence indicates that the EspP passenger domain is secreted in a hairpin conformation while distinct regions of the β domain interact with BamA, BamB and BamD (Ieva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C, with a citation.

claim: Proteolytic maturation and the release of the β domain from the Bam complex both require the completion of translocation.
source: In any case, the finding that proteolytic maturation and the release of the β domain from the Bam complex both require the completion of translocation (Peterson et al., 2010; Ieva et al., 2011; Pavlova et al., 2013) strongly suggests that the active site cannot form during the passage of the passenger domain across the OM.
evidence: This is stated in the text with citations.

claim: The active site cannot form during the passage of the passenger domain across the OM.
source: In any case, the finding that proteolytic maturation and the release of the β domain from the Bam complex both require the completion of translocation (Peterson et al., 2010; Ieva et al., 2011; Pavlova et al., 2013) strongly suggests that the active site cannot form during the passage of the passenger domain across the OM.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited findings.

claim: OmpT folded much more efficiently in the presence of BamABCDE than Bam(AB)(CDE).
source: Remarkably, the intensity of the fluorescent signal in the fluorogenic peptide cleavage assay indicated that OmpT folded much more efficiently in the presence of BamABCDE than Bam(AB)(CDE) (Figure 2E, compare green and purple curves).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The activity of the Bam complex is optimized when all of the subunits are expressed together.
source: These results suggested that the activity of the Bam complex is optimized when all of the subunits are expressed together.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of BamABCDE and Bam(AB)(CDE) activity.

claim: ∼10–20% of the protein was typically assembled under our experimental conditions.
source: Quantitation of the relative fluorescent signal produced by the denatured form of the EspP β domain and unprocessed EspP(46+β) on Western blots indicated that ∼10–20% of the protein was typically assembled under our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the Western blot data.

claim: A moderate increase in efficiency was observed when the BamABCDE concentration was increased from 0.05 μM to 0.2 μM.
source: A moderate increase in efficiency was observed when the BamABCDE concentration was increased from 0.05 μM to 0.2 μM (the concentration used in the experiments described here), but no increase was observed at higher concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: If fresh substrate was added 5ʹ after the start of the incubation, the total yield of assembled EspP(46+β) increased in proportion to the amount of added substrate.
source: Interestingly, if we added fresh substrate 5ʹ after the start of the incubation, the total yield of assembled EspP(46+β) increased in proportion to the amount of added substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The Bam complex can catalyze multiple rounds of assembly in vitro.
source: This observation is consistent with other evidence that the Bam complex can catalyze multiple rounds of assembly in vitro (Hagan and Kahne, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and the observation about substrate addition.

claim: The efficiency of EspP(46+β) assembly was limited by the inherent ability of the denatured protein to remain assembly competent after dilution out of 8 M urea.
source: In light of our results, it is likely that the efficiency of EspP(46+β) assembly was limited by the inherent ability of the denatured protein to remain assembly competent after dilution out of 8 M urea.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the concentration dependence data.

claim: Nanodiscs are stabilized by two copies of the scaffold protein.
source: Because nanodiscs are stabilized by two copies of the scaffold protein (Denisov et al., 2004), however, this observation is consistent with the prediction that they contained a single copy of the Bam complex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denisov et al., 2004.

claim: The nanodiscs produced a single band on Blue Native PAGE that migrated only slightly slower than a BamABCDE monomer.
source: In addition, the nanodiscs produced a single band on Blue Native PAGE that migrated only slightly slower than a BamABCDE monomer (compare Figure 8C to Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from the Blue Native PAGE data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The ∼30 kDa passenger domain of EspP(HA-251+β) accumulated in parallel with the cleaved β domain.
source: Although the non-vesicular nature of nanodiscs precluded assessment of passenger domain translocation using a PK-sensitivity assay, we found that the ∼30 kDa passenger domain of EspP(HA-251+β) accumulated in parallel with the cleaved β domain (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: A Bam complex monomer is sufficient to catalyze autotransporter assembly.
source: These results not only provide evidence that a Bam complex monomer is sufficient to catalyze autotransporter assembly, but also show that the curvature of the proteoliposome membrane is not itself required for the assembly process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the nanodisc assembly data.
